segments.line: You're in a white room with a window, a bed you never use, and a camera in the corner. They feed you well. They test you every hour.
Your body is falling apart, quietly. Your hands shake.
Your words come out in the wrong order.
People who sleep less than six hours a night are about four times more likely to catch a cold.
You haven't slept at all. You have three colds. You sneeze, and the scientist behind the glass writes it down.
Then the man shows you a slide. Rats. In the nineteen-eighties, scientists kept rats awake on purpose, around the clock. Within about two to four weeks, every one of them died.
'Your record falls on day eleven', he says. 'Day twenty-one is the real question'.
That night, Ellie video calls you. She's in her pajamas, holding her teddy. 'Mum says you're helping scientists. Are you coming home?
I leave the hallway light on for you every night. Like you do for me'.
Behind her, you can see your bedroom. Your bed. Your pillow. Things you haven't touched in ten days.
And you decide. No record. You're going home, and you're going to learn to sleep again, even if your brain has forgotten how.
You pull off the wires, walk past the camera, and ask for the one thing nobody in the building expected.
'Can someone please turn off the lights'?
The man in the suit doesn't try to stop you. He just writes something in his folder, and smiles, like he already knew.
